title: Unit Column Adder
context: Grade 5, the pages on adding and subtracting measures. An adult sees column sums. What the pages are doing is making the carry and the borrow happen between units, where one of the larger unit is 1000 or 100 or 10 of the smaller one, not always 10.

writeup.why: Add measures in unit columns with a carry, add them as decimals in the larger unit, take one measure from another with a borrow, and find a boundary once every side is in one unit.
writeup.look: A frame of two unit columns with measures stacked in it, carry and borrow tiles that are dragged across, and on the last phase a shape with its sides in mixed units.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Unit Column Adder' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of columns worked. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The frame fills the left of the area from x 120 to x 760: two columns, the larger unit on the left and the smaller on the right, each 300 wide and headed by its unit name in violet, labelled Unit. The measures the question gives are stacked in rows at y 280 and y 360 in deep blue, labelled Given, with a ruled line at y 410 and the answer row at y 460. The smaller unit's column is worked first and is lit amber. The Bundle button stands at x 820, y 280 and the Break button at x 820, y 380; a carry or a borrow is a tile carrying a violet Unit fact, dragged between the columns. On the second phase the frame turns into decimal rows in the larger unit with the points locked in one line at x 440, and a grey zero, labelled Place holder, holds any empty place. A part taken away is rose, labelled Taken away. On the fourth phase the flower bed is drawn at x 160, y 240 inside a box 560 by 400, with each side card on its side and the walker a small drawn figure at a corner. Every answer is green, labelled Answer, with its unit. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a point key, a delete key, and a key for each unit in use. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the nine tools of this chapter share them. The measure the question gives, in the unit it is given in, is deep blue, labelled Given or Measure. The measure the working reaches, and a reading on a scale, is green, labelled Answer, Reading or Same measure. The places moved across the unit chart, and the worth of one small mark on a scale, are vermilion, labelled Move or One mark. A unit fact, the unit names on the chart and the other temperature scale are violet, labelled Unit fact, Unit or Other scale. The part taken away, and a part left over after sharing, are rose, labelled Taken away or Left over. The unit, column, mark or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open inside a number, labelled Place holder, and for nothing else. Rulers, tapes, jugs, scales, thermometer tubes, chart lines, arrows, operation signs and step labels are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of the content colours, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last working stays in the frame, with its carry or borrow tile where the child dropped it and the answer in green.

phases.win: the bundle lands in the metres column and the sum turns green
phases.does: adds the centimetres, bundles a metre out of them, drags it across, then adds the metres
phases.goal: add the smaller unit first, and carry one of the larger unit across when the smaller column fills up
phases.says: Smaller unit first. Is there a whole metre in there?
phases.check: Away from the screen: how many centimetres make one metre, and so when do you carry?
phases.feels: a full column wrapping itself into one bundle and hopping across
phases.hands: Write two lengths in metres and centimetres on squared paper in two columns. Add the centimetres first, and if there is a whole metre in them, carry it into the metres column.
phases.tries: First rung: add only the centimetres column. Second rung: bundle a metre out of it. Third rung: the same task on two lengths whose centimetres do not reach a metre, before the question's own lengths return.

wrong.why: the column total is just what the adding gave, as it is in a column of ones
wrong.move: writes the centimetres total, a hundred or more, as it stands in the centimetres column
wrong.screen: the over-full total stays in its column lit amber, and the Bundle button beside it is lit until a bundle is made from it

wrong.why: in reading, the left comes first, so the larger unit feels like the place to start
wrong.move: adds the metres column first and forgets the carry
wrong.screen: the metres total stays, the centimetres column is lit amber, and once its bundle is made the carry tile waits beside the metres column

phases.screen: two lengths in metres and centimetres stacked in the frame
phases.soWhat: add the smaller unit first, and carry one of the larger unit across when the smaller column fills up

phases.win: the decimal answer turns green, with the word litres beside it
phases.does: writes each capacity as a decimal in litres, lines up the points, adds, and names the unit
phases.goal: write each measure as a decimal in the larger unit, line up the points and add; the answer is in the larger unit
phases.says: Points in a line. Which unit is the answer in?
phases.check: Away from the screen: why must the points be in one line before you add?
phases.feels: the points lining up like buttons and the answer landing in litres
phases.hands: Write two capacities as decimals in litres, one under the other, with the points in one line. Add as with any decimals, and write litres beside the answer.
phases.tries: First rung: write only the first capacity as a decimal in litres. Second rung: write the second under it. Third rung: the same task with no empty place after the point, before the question's own capacities return.

wrong.why: the millilitres look like they go straight after the point
wrong.move: writes a capacity's millilitres straight after the point with no zero in an empty place
wrong.screen: that row is read back in litres and millilitres beside it, showing more millilitres than the question gave, and the empty place is lit amber with a grey zero waiting

wrong.why: the question was written with millilitres in it, so that unit feels right
wrong.move: names the decimal answer in millilitres
wrong.screen: the answer waits uncoloured, and the unit the rows are in, litres, is lit amber above the frame

phases.screen: two capacities in litres and millilitres, and the decimal rows waiting
phases.soWhat: write each measure as a decimal in the larger unit, line up the points and add; the answer is in the larger unit

phases.win: the rose part is taken away, and what is left turns green
phases.does: breaks one kilogram into grams, drags them across, then takes away column by column
phases.goal: when there is too little of the smaller unit, change one of the larger unit into the smaller unit first
phases.says: Not enough grams. Break a kilogram.
phases.check: Away from the screen: when you break one metre for a borrow, how many centimetres do you get?
phases.feels: one kilogram breaking into a heap of grams that makes the taking away possible
phases.hands: Write a weight in kilograms and grams, and a smaller one under it that needs more grams than the top has. Cross out one kilogram, write the grams it becomes, then take away.
phases.tries: First rung: take away the grams where there are enough. Second rung: break one kilogram and count the grams. Third rung: the same task on lengths in metres and centimetres, before the question's own weights return.

wrong.why: in each column the bigger number seems as if it should go on top
wrong.move: takes the smaller grams number from the larger, whichever row it is in
wrong.screen: the grams column is shown too short beside the part to be taken away, both lit amber, and the child's column total stays

wrong.why: every take away starts to feel like it needs a borrow
wrong.move: presses Break when there are already enough grams
wrong.screen: the broken kilogram's tile waits beside the grams column, the two grams parts are laid side by side so the child sees there were enough, and the tile can be dragged back

phases.screen: a weight in kilograms and grams, and a smaller weight to take away that needs more grams than are there
phases.soWhat: when there is too little of the smaller unit, change one of the larger unit into the smaller unit first

phases.win: the walker comes home, and the boundary turns green in metres
phases.does: taps each side card to rewrite it in metres, then sets the walker going round
phases.goal: write every side in the unit asked for, then add all the sides
phases.says: Every side in metres first. Then walk round.
phases.check: Away from the screen: before you add the sides of a shape, what must be true of every side?
phases.feels: the walker coming home and the whole boundary turning green
phases.hands: Draw a four-sided shape and label its sides in two or three units. Rewrite every side in metres on a strip of paper, then add the strips.
phases.tries: First rung: rewrite one side card in metres. Second rung: rewrite the rest. Third rung: the same task on a triangle with two units, before the question's own shape returns.

wrong.why: the numbers are all there, ready to add
wrong.move: sets the walker going while some side cards are still in their own units
wrong.screen: the side left in its own unit stays on its card, lit amber, while the walker waits at that corner

wrong.why: centimetres to metres is two places, and that step sticks in the mind
wrong.move: rewrites a side in millimetres by moving the point only two places
wrong.screen: the side card reads back in the unit its point now sits after, and that side is drawn to scale beside the real side so the two lengths are seen apart

phases.screen: a four-sided flower bed with its sides labelled in metres, centimetres and millimetres
phases.soWhat: write every side in the unit asked for, then add all the sides

writeup.delight: On the first phase, when the Bundle button wraps the full column, the bundle is tied with a small violet ribbon carrying the unit fact and hops over into the larger column.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet worked. On the first phase two lengths in metres and centimetres stand stacked in the frame. On the second two capacities in litres and millilitres stand beside empty decimal rows. On the third a weight in kilograms and grams stands above a smaller weight to take away. On the fourth a four-sided flower bed lies with each side labelled in its own unit and a walker at one corner. One thing moves, once: the smaller unit's column, the first decimal row, the Break button or the first side card gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any measures stacked in the frame and added or taken away, in columns or as decimals, and any shape walked round. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on carries, decimal sums, borrows and boundaries.
voiceLines: Two measures, stacked in their unit columns.
Smaller unit first. Is there a whole metre in there?

Not enough grams. Break a kilogram.
Every side in metres first. Then walk round.

observations.why: enough of the smaller unit makes one of the larger unit.
observations.soWhat: carry it across, as in whole-number sums, with the unit fact as the size of the bundle.
observations.observe: The smaller unit's column filled past one of the larger unit, and the Bundle button lit.

observations.why: each row was written as a decimal in the larger unit before adding.
observations.soWhat: line up the points, and name the unit the rows are in.
observations.observe: With the points in one line, the decimal sum ended in the larger unit.

observations.why: the unit fact, not ten, says how many of the smaller unit make one larger unit.
observations.soWhat: a borrow across units uses the unit fact of those two units.
observations.observe: A broken larger unit filled the smaller column with far more than ten.

observations.why: sides in different units cannot be added as they stand.
observations.soWhat: rewrite every side in one unit, then add them all.
observations.observe: The walker would not move past a side still in its own unit.

serves.exercise: finding four sums of measures in units and as decimals
finding four differences of measures written as decimals
finding the total distance three people travelled
finding the cloth left after two pieces are given away
finding the boundary of a kitchen in metres from sides in mixed units

source_tool.description: A frame of two unit columns fills the working area, the larger unit on the left and the smaller on the right, each headed by its unit name in violet. The measures the question gives are stacked in the frame in deep blue, labelled Given. The smaller unit's column is worked first and is lit amber. When its total reaches one of the larger unit, a Bundle button wraps that much into one tile labelled with the violet unit fact, such as 1 kg = 1000 g, and the child drags it into the larger column as a carry. On the second phase the frame turns into decimal rows in the larger unit, with the points locked in one line and a grey zero holding any empty place. On the third phase a Break button turns one of the larger unit into the smaller unit, which the child drags across as a borrow, and the part taken away is rose, labelled Taken away. On the fourth phase a shape is drawn with each side labelled in its own unit, and each side card is rewritten in the unit asked for before a walker goes round the boundary adding. Every answer is green, labelled Answer, with its unit. The running count at the top left of the canvas counts the columns worked.
source_tool.art_direction: Tapes and scales on a workbench / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a unit chart of seven columns from kilo to milli with the base unit in the middle, rulers and tapes marked in their units, kitchen scales, measuring jugs marked in millilitres, and thermometers with labelled marks.
Every measure is written with its unit on every line, and every decimal names the unit it is in, so 3.04 L is never shown as a bare 3.04.
Every mixed measure shown is ordinary: its smaller part is less than one of the larger unit.
Places are counted from the unit the child has to the unit the child wants, one hop at a time, and each hop shows the number, not the unit, divided or multiplied by 10.
Multiplying and dividing a measure happen in its smallest unit, in whole numbers, and a sharing that does not come out even shows what is left over.
A thermometer shows what one small mark is worth before its column is read, and a Celsius reading sits beside a Fahrenheit one only in the four pairs the chapter prints.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a hop across the chart, a carry across units, a length shared into equal pieces, or a column rising to a mark.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a unit or a mark the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a measure plays in a piece of working: the measure the question gives is deep blue, and the measure the working reaches, with a reading taken off a scale, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The places moved across the unit chart, each one dividing or multiplying the number by 10, and the worth of one small mark on a scale are vermilion. A unit fact such as 1 kg = 1000 g, the unit names on the chart and the other temperature scale are violet. The part taken away, and a remainder left over after sharing, are rose. The unit, column, mark or step being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Move, Unit fact, Taken away, Left over and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the smaller unit's column. Is there a whole larger unit in it?
voice.opening: Two measures, stacked in their unit columns.
voice.onFinish: You added and took away, one unit column at a time.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Stack any measures and add or take away.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has weighed two bags of books, added the weights in columns and then weighed both bags together. The tool is what bundles and breaks the units by hand, which a finished column sum on paper cannot show.

answer_key.rule: Add the smaller unit first. When it reaches one of the larger unit, carry that one across: 1000 g make 1 kg, 100 cm make 1 m, 1000 mL make 1 litre. When there is too little of the smaller unit to take away, change one of the larger unit into the smaller unit first. To add or take away as decimals, write every measure in the larger unit and line up the points; the decimal answer is in that larger unit. For a boundary, write every side in the unit asked for, then add all the sides.
answer_key.wrong: The stage keeps the child's working. A column left over-full stays as it is, with its total lit amber until a bundle is made from it. A borrow not made shows the smaller column too short beside the part to be taken away, both lit amber. A side left in its own unit stays on its card, lit amber, while the walker waits at that corner. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: 123 cm is 1 m 23 cm, so write 23 cm and carry 1 m.
Add the metres with the carry: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7.
So together they are 7 m 23 cm long.
items.question: Two pieces of wire are 4 m 65 cm and 2 m 58 cm long. How long are they together?
items.checkpoint: Add the smaller unit first, and carry one of the larger unit across when the smaller column fills up.
items.misconception: Writing all of the centimetres in the centimetre column and never carrying the metre across, so the centimetres hold more than a metre.

steps: Write each in litres: 5 L 340 mL is 5.340 L, and 1 L 785 mL is 1.785 L.
Line up the points and add: 5.340 + 1.785 = 7.125.
The decimal is in litres, the larger unit.
So together they hold 7.125 L, and 7 L 125 mL is 7.125 L.
items.question: A jug holds 5 L 340 mL and a bottle holds 1 L 785 mL. Add them as decimals in litres.
items.checkpoint: The decimal answer is in the larger unit, and that unit is written with it.
items.misconception: Writing the decimal with mL after it, which turns more than seven litres into a few drops.

steps: There are not enough grams to take 580 g from 240 g.
That leaves 5 in the kilogram column, and 5 - 3 = 2.
So 2 kg 660 g of paint is left.
items.question: A drum held 6 kg 240 g of paint, and 3 kg 580 g was used. How much is left?
items.checkpoint: When there is too little of the smaller unit, change one of the larger unit into the smaller unit first.
items.misconception: Taking 240 from 580 in the gram column because it is easier, which leaves more paint than is really there.

steps: First write every side in metres.
450 cm is 4.5 m, and 4500 mm is 4.5 m.
items.question: A flower bed has sides of 7 m, 450 cm, 7 m and 4500 mm. What is its boundary in metres?
items.checkpoint: For a boundary, write every side in the unit asked for, then add all the sides.
items.misconception: Adding the four numbers as they stand, mixing metres, centimetres and millimetres, which gives a boundary thousands of metres long.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Add 2 kg 300 g and 1 kg 500 g.
Write 3 m 45 cm as a decimal in metres, ready to add.
When 1 kg is broken into grams for a borrow, how many grams is that?
Add 3 km 640 m and 2 km 755 m.
Take 1 m 75 cm from 4 m 30 cm.
A triangle of card has sides of 60 cm, 0.8 m and 1000 mm. What is its boundary in metres?
A roll had 15 m 20 cm of tape, and 6 m 85 cm was used. How much is left?

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: wraps one of the larger unit's worth of the smaller unit into a carry tile
turns one of the larger unit into the smaller unit for a borrow
moves a carry or a borrow between the columns
is tapped to rewrite a side in the unit asked for
types a column total, a decimal or an answer

teaching_notes: Add the smaller unit first and carry when it fills up; say how many of the smaller unit make one of the larger each time, because it is 1000, 100 or 10 depending on the units. When borrowing, change one larger unit into the smaller unit and say how many that is. Adding as decimals needs every measure in the larger unit with the points lined up, and the answer's decimal is in that unit. For a boundary, rewrite every side in the unit asked for before adding. Bring in labels from packets at home and add their measures here.
generation_prompt: Build a measure column tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A frame of two unit columns, larger unit on the left, headed in violet, holds measures stacked in deep blue. The smaller column is worked first and lit amber. A Bundle button wraps one of the larger unit's worth into a tile carrying the violet unit fact, which the child drags into the larger column; a Break button turns one of the larger unit into the smaller unit for a borrow, and the part taken away is rose. The second phase shows decimal rows in the larger unit with the points locked in a line and grey zeros holding empty places.
